Wong et al. (2017)
Western Siberia; northeastern Europe; Urals
Mansi, Khanty, Nenets, Selkup and other northern Eurasian groups; published Yamnaya and other ancient comparators
Modern genomes; ancient comparators include Yamnaya (~4.7–5.3 kya)
28 high-coverage modern genomes from 14 groups, 32 additional modern genomes and 46 published ancient genomes
High-coverage whole-genome sequencing; PCA; TreeMix; D-statistics; admixture modelling
Western Siberian groups, especially Mansi, share excess alleles with ancient eastern Europeans including Yamnaya; western Siberian-related ancestry is also detectable in northeastern Europeans.
Western Siberia / Urals
Northeastern and eastern Europe
Westward gene flow and later contact across northern Eurasia
Authors infer western Siberian input into northeastern Europe before the Yamnaya horizon, probably before ~6.6 kya.
Admixture and allele-sharing; not a directly sampled Yamnaya migration transect
The authors reconstruct deep Siberia–Europe interaction and caution that Mansi are not descendants of Yamnaya.
BACKGROUND
Late Proto-Indo-European is contextual only; the paper makes no independent linguistic inference.
Genetic statements are direct results plus author demographic interpretation; language is background attributed to cited literature.
Predominantly a northern Eurasian study using modern populations; target-period movement is indirect.
Ancient genomes are published comparators; direction and timing depend on population models and sparse ancient sampling.
Adds contextual evidence that northern Eurasian gene flow pre-dated and overlapped the Yamnaya horizon, qualifying a simple one-way expansion narrative.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION
pp. 1–2, 9–12

Chintalapati et al. (2022)
Europe and western Asia; 16 regional groupings
Mesolithic, Neolithic, Steppe pastoralist, Yamnaya/Afanasievo-related and later European populations
~8000–350 BCE
Approximately 1,100 published ancient individuals
DATES ancestry-covariance dating; ancestry source modelling; regional meta-analysis
Admixture-date estimates reconstruct the formation and spread of Steppe pastoralist ancestry; estimated Yamnaya/Afanasievo genetic formation precedes their archaeological appearance by more than a millennium.
Pontic-Caspian Steppe and related eastern sources
Multiple European regions and the Altai
Multi-stage westward and eastward dispersal of Steppe ancestry
Formation before the Yamnaya horizon; major dispersals around and after ~3000 BCE
Dated ancestry mixture and regional shifts
The authors interpret the dated admixture patterns as a reconstruction of major Holocene migrations.
EXPLICIT
The demographic chronology is presented as relevant to competing models of Indo-European dispersal; DNA does not identify the language spoken.
Admixture dates are direct model outputs; migration and language links are author interpretations.
Very broad spatial and temporal coverage; regional sampling density is uneven and much evidence lies outside 3300–2600 BCE.
DATES approximates pulse admixture; multiple pulses can yield intermediate dates, closely related sources are difficult to separate and low ancestry proportions are uncertain.
Provides a comparative chronology for Steppe-related ancestry formation and its westward/eastward spread.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION + LANGUAGE
pp. 1–6 and regional-results sections
Treat linguistic relevance as interpretation of the demographic timeline.


Wang et al. (2021)
Mongolia, northern China, Amur region and western China
Yamnaya/Afanasievo-related groups, Chemurchek, Shirenzigou and other ancient East Asian populations
~6000 BCE–AD 1000
166 ancient individuals and 383 present-day individuals from 46 groups
Genome-wide capture / sequencing; PCA; qpWave; qpAdm; qpGraph; ancestry modelling
Afanasievo is genetically very close to Yamnaya; Yamnaya/Afanasievo-related ancestry reached western Mongolia after ~3000 BCE, later declined there and persisted farther west in Xinjiang.
Pontic-Caspian Steppe via Afanasievo-associated eastern groups
Altai, western Mongolia and Xinjiang
Eastward Steppe dispersal with later regional admixture and partial ancestry loss
After ~3000 BCE, with later Bronze and Iron Age continuities
Appearance of Yamnaya/Afanasievo-related ancestry, admixture and regional turnover
The authors interpret the genetic links as evidence for movement of Yamnaya descendants into Inner Asia.
EXPLICIT
The authors argue that the demographic evidence adds weight to a migration-mediated spread of proto-Tocharian; this remains an interdisciplinary inference.
Ancestry estimates are direct genetic results; the Tocharian link is author interpretation.
East Asian ancient-DNA sampling is uneven, with several small or singleton archaeological groups; most evidence is east of the core Yamnaya zone.
Some qpAdm models are equally plausible and closely related sources can be difficult to distinguish; cultural association does not guarantee matching ancestry.
Supplies the principal eastward case study and an explicit, qualified Tocharian interpretation.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION + LANGUAGE
pp. 1, 4–6
An Afanasievo-associated child without Yamnaya ancestry illustrates culture–ancestry non-equivalence.


Scorrano et al. (2021)
Central, eastern, western and southern Europe
Yamnaya proxies; Corded Ware; Bell Beaker; Neolithic and Bronze Age Europeans
Late Neolithic to Bronze Age, focused on the third millennium BCE
Published genome-wide and uniparental datasets; mtDNA phylogeny includes 695 samples; analysis-specific sample sizes vary
PCA; qpAdm; outgroup f3; mtDNA and Y-chromosome analysis; autosome-versus-X ancestry comparison
Steppe-related ancestry is highest in several Corded Ware groups and is more strongly male-biased there than in Bell Beaker groups; no comparable significant Steppe input is detected in the pooled mitochondrial gene pool.
Pontic-Caspian Steppe
Primarily central and eastern Europe, with weaker or heterogeneous signals farther west and south
Westward, sex-biased ancestry dispersal followed by regionally variable admixture
Mainly early to middle third millennium BCE
High Steppe ancestry, sex-biased admixture and partial paternal-line replacement
The authors interpret the autosomal, X-chromosomal and uniparental differences as predominantly male-driven migration, especially into Corded Ware groups.
INDIRECT
The discussion treats Steppe ancestry as compatible with the spread of some Indo-European languages but also notes counterexamples; language is not measured.
Genetic proportions are direct/modelled results; migration and language connections are author interpretation.
Coverage is strongest for central/eastern Europe and varies sharply by regional archaeological group.
Published-data reanalysis; low X-chromosome SNP counts and large standard deviations require caution; Yamnaya Y lineages are an imperfect male-source proxy.
Provides a focused test of sex-biased migration and cautions against assuming the same demographic process across all of Europe.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION
pp. 1–3, 7–9
Language discussion is secondary and should not change the section classification.


Linderholm et al. (2020)
Southeastern Poland: Rzeszów Foothills, Małopolska Upland and Sokal Ridge
Corded Ware and Bell Beaker individuals; Neolithic local and Steppe-related ancestry components
Late third millennium BCE; individual radiocarbon dates reported
19 genomes obtained from 53 sampled individuals (16 Corded Ware, 3 Bell Beaker); strontium for 16 individuals
Whole-genome sequencing; PCA and ancestry analysis; mtDNA/Y haplogroups; kinship; strontium isotopes; radiocarbon dating
Corded Ware individuals combine predominantly Steppe-associated paternal ancestry with maternal lineages linked to earlier Neolithic populations; three kin relationships include a local/non-local pair.
Eastern Steppe-related ancestry
Southeastern Poland
Westward ancestry movement followed by local admixture and community-level mobility
Corded Ware dominance after ~2800 BCE; sampled burials lie in the later third millennium BCE
Admixture, sex-biased ancestry, kinship and isotope-based local/non-local mobility
The authors interpret the combined evidence as a complex, regionally specific Corded Ware community rather than a homogeneous migrant population.
INDIRECT
Linguistic change is mentioned as part of the broader third-millennium transition; no independent language analysis is performed.
Genomic and isotope observations are direct results; wider migration and language statements are author interpretation/background.
A single regional transect in southeastern Poland cannot represent all Corded Ware populations.
Small sample size and uneven genome coverage (~0.02× to 5.47×); isotope baselines and cultural labels constrain mobility interpretation.
Adds fine-scale evidence for sex-biased ancestry, local admixture and mobility within a Corded Ware community.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION
pp. 1–4 and Results/Discussion
Useful for qualifying continent-wide replacement models with community-level complexity.


Tassi et al. (2017)
Kierzkowo, northwestern Poland; central European comparison
Globular Amphorae culture, earlier Neolithic farmers, Yamnaya/Steppe-related groups and Corded Ware
GAC context before the main Steppe expansion, approximately 3400/3100–2800 BCE
Six individuals with nuclear data at 597,573 SNPs and 11 complete Neolithic mitochondrial sequences
Genome-wide comparison; PCA and allele-sharing statistics; mitochondrial analysis; approximate Bayesian computation of alternative demographic models
Sampled GAC individuals are closer to earlier Neolithic groups than to populations related to Pontic-Steppe migration and lack the expected Yamnaya-derived profile.
No supported Yamnaya-derived origin for the sampled GAC group
Northwestern Poland / central Europe
Local genetic continuity with eastern cultural influence, before later Steppe gene flow
Immediately before and overlapping the start of the target period
Continuity and absence of expected Steppe ancestry; later gene flow is not rejected
The authors interpret GAC eastern archaeological affinities as cultural influence rather than movement of Steppe people.
EXPLICIT
The study tests demographic expectations of Steppe/Kurgan and Anatolian language-dispersal models and stresses that language change need not track migration exactly.
Genetic model comparison is direct; implications for Indo-European dispersal are author interpretation.
One burial context in northwestern Poland and a small number of individuals limit geographic generalization.
Small sample; preservation and sample-selection losses; demographic conclusions depend on the compared models and reference populations.
Provides a negative/qualifying case showing that archaeological eastern affinity need not imply Steppe migration or linguistic identity.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION + LANGUAGE
pp. 1–4, 6–8
Use to separate cultural transmission from demic diffusion.


Ringbauer et al. (2024)
Eurasia, with a focused Corded Ware–Yamnaya analysis
Yamnaya, Corded Ware, Globular Amphora and other Eneolithic/Bronze Age groups
Broad ancient dataset; relevant Corded Ware interval ~3000–2400 BCE
4,248 ancient Eurasian individuals
ancIBD hidden Markov model; GLIMPSE imputation/phasing; identity-by-descent segment analysis
Corded Ware groups share long IBD segments, including segments up to 20 cM, with multiple Yamnaya groups; most Corded Ware ancestry has genealogical links to Yamnaya within at most a few hundred years, alongside a substantial GAC-related component.
Pontic-Caspian Steppe plus eastern European GAC-related ancestry
Eastern, central and northern European Corded Ware groups
Rapid, connected westward/northward dispersal followed by admixture
Gene flow beginning around 3000 BCE; relationships span only a few hundred years
Recent co-ancestry, direct genealogical links and admixture
The authors interpret long IBD sharing as inconsistent with a remote unsampled Steppe-like source separated from Yamnaya by about a millennium.
INDIRECT
The study provides a demographic mechanism relevant to language spread but makes no independent claim about which language sampled people spoke.
IBD segments are direct model outputs; migration is author interpretation; any linguistic use is later synthesis.
Results depend on which ancient individuals pass coverage thresholds and on uneven archaeological sampling.
Reliable detection is mainly for segments >8 cM and adequate coverage; SNP density, low coverage, imputation and false positives limit shorter-segment inference.
Strengthens the immediate genealogical connection between Yamnaya and diverse Corded Ware populations.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION
pp. 1, 5, 7–8
No independent linguistic evidence.


Dzhaubermezov et al. (2026)
North and South Caucasus
Caucasus hunter-gatherers, Maykop, Yamnaya, Catacomb, Kura-Araxes and later Caucasus populations
~50,000 BCE–AD 1914; Bronze Age evidence is the relevant subset
669 ancient individuals compiled; 565 ancient Caucasus individuals retained for PCA after quality control; modern comparators also used
Systematic synthesis of published datasets; quality-controlled pooled reanalysis; PCA; D-statistics; relatedness screening
The pooled data show early north–south differentiation, Bronze Age Steppe-related gene flow associated with Yamnaya and later admixture alongside substantial regional continuity.
Eurasian Steppe and eastern Europe
Caucasus populations
Corridor-like, bidirectional interaction across and around the Caucasus
Long-term prehistory; Yamnaya-linked signal concentrated in the Bronze Age
Gene flow, admixture, differentiation and continuity
The authors synthesize the Caucasus as both a barrier and migration corridor involved in the ancestry of Steppe pastoralist societies.
BACKGROUND
Proto-Indo-Anatolian and language–genetics links are largely attributed to recent cited studies rather than independently tested.
Pooled genetic patterns are reanalysis results; many detailed migration and language claims are synthesis or attribution to source studies.
Extremely broad chronology; early North Caucasus and late historical sampling gaps; Bronze Age findings must be isolated from later continuity.
Secondary data vary in coverage, laboratory pipelines and sampling; pooled PCA is descriptive; source-study overlap risks double counting.
Provides Caucasus corridor context and a secondary cross-study check on Steppe-related gene flow.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION
pp. 1–4 and Bronze Age/Conclusion sections
Zotero issue-date metadata is later than the audit date and remains flagged for citation verification.


Lazaridis et al. (2025)
Caucasus–Lower Volga, Volga, Dnipro, Pontic-Caspian Steppe and southeast Europe
Caucasus–Lower Volga cline, Volga cline, Dnipro cline, Serednii Stih, Yamnaya, Corded Ware and Anatolian-related groups
~6400–2000 BCE
435 individuals (367 newly reported plus 68 with improved data); 803 libraries screened
Genome-wide ancient DNA; PCA; qpWave/qpAdm competition framework; admixture dating; IBD and haplogroup analyses
Caucasus–Lower Volga ancestry moved west and mixed with Dnipro/Don hunter-gatherer ancestry, contributing about four-fifths of Yamnaya ancestry; a Core Yamnaya population formed by ~4000 BCE and expanded rapidly after ~3300 BCE.
Caucasus–Lower Volga and lower Dnipro/Don interaction zone
Pontic-Caspian Steppe, Danube corridor, southeastern Europe and east to Kazakhstan
Multi-stage formation followed by rapid westward and eastward expansion
Precursors ~4500–4000 BCE; Yamnaya expansion after ~3300 BCE
Admixture, ancestry clines, rapid demographic expansion and later local admixture
The authors propose a lower Dnipro/Don-centred formation process and a rapid Yamnaya expansion, while acknowledging unresolved core geography.
EXPLICIT
The authors propose proto-Indo-Anatolian unity among Caucasus–Lower Volga populations before Yamnaya formation and link later dispersals to language branching.
Ancestry models are direct genetic results; migration routes and proto-Indo-Anatolian reconstruction are interdisciplinary author interpretations.
More than 80% of the study samples are from Russia; lower Volga precursors and some proposed routes remain sparsely sampled.
An unsampled CHG-related source is required in models; precise Anatolian route/source and Core Yamnaya location cannot be fixed conclusively.
Provides the central formation-and-expansion model and the collection’s strongest explicit genetics–language synthesis.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION + LANGUAGE
pp. 1–7
Use the canonical Zotero item; DHIHCURJ is an exact duplicate.


Nikitin et al. (2025)
North Pontic region, especially present-day Ukraine
North Pontic foragers, Trypillian farmers, Usatove, Serednii Stih and Yamna
Neolithic to Early Bronze Age; key interval ~4500–3300 BCE
81 prehistoric North Pontic individuals; 51 direct radiocarbon dates; co-analysis with the companion Steppe dataset
Genome-wide ancient DNA; PCA; qpAdm/ancestry modelling; radiocarbon and isotope context
Three ancestry-bearing movements are resolved: Caucasus–Lower Volga migrants mixing with Trypillians to form Usatove, a parallel mixture with foragers forming Serednii Stih, and Yamna descent from Serednii Stih with expansion from ~3300 BCE.
Caucasus–Lower Volga and North Pontic interaction zones
Usatove/North Pontic sites and then wider Eurasia
Successive westward/local mixtures followed by Yamna expansion
~4500 BCE, ~4000 BCE formation, and ~3300 BCE expansion
Admixture, ancestry replacement and repeated incorporation of outsiders
The authors interpret the three waves as a flexible demographic strategy underlying Yamna success and expansion.
INDIRECT
Indo-European dispersal is contextual; the paper reconstructs a plausible population mechanism but does not directly identify language.
Genetic mixtures are direct/modelled results; migration-wave framing is author interpretation; language link is contextual.
Concentrated in the North Pontic region and dependent on site availability; the wider Eurasian expansion is inferred using companion data.
Some proximate ancestry sources remain unclear; uneven earlier sampling and model dependence limit fine-scale route certainty.
Supplies high-resolution evidence for Yamnaya formation immediately before, and expansion at the start of, the target period.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION
pp. 1–4 and Discussion
Mykhailivka individual (3635–3383 BCE) bridges the Serednii Stih–Yamna temporal gap.


Papac et al. (2021)
Bohemia, central Europe
Pre-Corded Ware groups, Corded Ware, Bell Beaker and Únětice populations
~4900–1600 BCE; key evidence ~2900–2400 BCE
271 ancient human genomes
Genome-wide ancient DNA; PCA; f-statistics/qpAdm; haplogroups; kinship and temporal population modelling
Corded Ware appears by ~2900 BCE with high but heterogeneous Steppe ancestry not wholly derived from sampled Yamnaya; diverse females were assimilated, followed by sharp Y-chromosome changes around 2600 and 2400 BCE and later ≥40% turnover.
Eastern Steppe-related sources and local central European groups
Bohemia
Westward arrival followed by local assimilation and repeated social/genetic reorganization
~2900 BCE arrival; transformations around 2600 and 2400 BCE; later Bronze Age turnover
Migration, admixture, sex-biased incorporation and partial population replacement
The authors interpret the Bohemian transect as evidence for multiple migrations and changing social structures, not a single homogeneous replacement.
INDIRECT
The population movements could carry language, but the study does not independently determine linguistic identity.
Genetic changes are direct/modelled results; migration and social implications are author interpretation; any language connection is later synthesis.
One central-European region; later 2400 BCE and Bronze Age evidence lies outside the primary 3300–2600 BCE interval.
Archaeological culture labels may not represent unified social entities; source populations remain partly unsampled and ancestry models are proxy-dependent.
Provides a regional time transect that qualifies simple mass-replacement and single-source accounts.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION
pp. 1–6
Clearly label post-2600 BCE results as later consequences.


Mathieson et al. (2018)
Balkan Peninsula, Carpathian Basin, North Pontic Steppe and surrounding southeastern Europe
Hunter-gatherers, Neolithic farmers, Eneolithic groups and Yamnaya-related Steppe populations
~12,000–500 BCE; relevant Steppe contacts extend into the fourth and third millennia BCE
225 ancient individuals (215 newly reported); 216 retained for population analysis after exclusions
1.24-million-SNP capture; PCA; supervised/unsupervised ADMIXTURE; D-statistics; qpAdm; qpGraph; 137 new radiocarbon dates
Intermittent genetic contact between southeastern Europe and Steppe populations occurred up to ~2,000 years before the large Steppe migrations; the dataset also documents early stages of Steppe ancestry formation and later ancestry replacement.
North Pontic / Eurasian Steppe
Southeastern Europe and, in later comparison, northern Europe
Repeated east–west contact preceding larger third-millennium migration
Early contacts before 4000 BCE; major later movements around and after 3000 BCE
Gene flow, admixture, ancestry formation and later replacement
The authors interpret southeastern Europe as a long-term east–west nexus rather than a corridor activated only by the Yamnaya expansion.
INDIRECT
The study supplies demographic context relevant to language-spread models but does not make language an empirical outcome.
Ancestry signals are direct/modelled results; migration interpretation is author inference; linguistic use is later synthesis.
Chronology is extremely broad and much evidence predates or postdates 3300–2600 BCE; relevant subsets must be isolated.
Uneven preservation and coverage, thresholds for analysed individuals and proxy-based ancestry models constrain fine-scale conclusions.
Shows that Yamnaya-era movement emerged from a longer history of Steppe–southeastern European contact.
INCLUDE - MIGRATION
pp. 1–4 and Steppe-contact sections
Do not conflate early contact with the later mass-migration phase.


Olalde et al. (2018)
Western and central Europe, especially Iberia, central Europe and Britain
Bell Beaker-associated individuals, Corded Ware-related Steppe ancestry and local Neolithic populations
~4700–800 BCE; key Beaker interval ~2750–2200 BCE
400 ancient Europeans from 136 sites, including 226 Beaker-associated individuals; combined analysis dataset 683 ancient samples
1.23-million-SNP capture; PCA; f-statistics/qpAdm; Y-chromosome analysis; 111 direct radiocarbon dates
Iberian and central-European Beaker groups show limited genetic affinity, but Beaker-associated migration carried high Steppe-related ancestry into Britain and replaced about 90% of its gene pool within a few hundred years.
Central/northern European Steppe-related populations
Western Europe, especially Britain
Continued east-to-west dispersal with regionally different balances of cultural diffusion and migration
From ~2750/2500 BCE, mainly after the primary Yamnaya interval
Regional non-migration, major migration elsewhere and near-total population replacement in Britain
The authors interpret the Beaker phenomenon as heterogeneous: cultural transmission between some regions and mass migration into others.
INDIRECT
The study demonstrates a later demographic mechanism that could transmit language but makes no independent language identification.
Genetic affinities and turnover are direct/modelled results; cultural-diffusion versus migration conclusions are author interpretation.
Most decisive British evidence postdates 2600 BCE and represents consequences of earlier Steppe dispersal, not core Yamnaya movement.
Regional sample imbalance and proxy ancestry sources limit exact origins; shared artefacts cannot be equated with shared population identity.
Provides a strong later consequence and a clear demonstration that material-culture spread can be demic in one region and cultural in another.

pp. 1–5
Use as a late-target/post-target consequence, not as direct evidence of Yamnaya speakers.


Allentoft et al. (2015)
Europe and central Asia
Yamnaya, Corded Ware, Afanasievo and other Bronze Age Eurasian groups
Broadly ~3000–1000 BCE, with relevant early Bronze Age samples
101 low-coverage ancient Eurasian genomes; 19 exceed 1× average coverage
Low-coverage whole-genome sequencing; PCA; ADMIXTURE; f-statistics; genomic-distance and haplogroup analysis
Corded Ware groups show substantial Yamnaya-related ancestry, while Afanasievo individuals in the Altai are genetically close to Yamnaya, documenting both westward and eastward Steppe-associated dispersals.
Pontic-Caspian Steppe
Central/northern Europe and the Altai / central Asia
Large-scale bidirectional expansion followed by mixture and regional replacement
Early third millennium BCE and later Bronze Age consequences
Ancestry appearance, admixture and population replacement

Low and uneven genome coverage; source populations are proxies and cultural labels may encompass heterogeneous populations.

pp. 1–5

Haak et al. (2015)
Central and northern Europe with Yamnaya samples from Samara
Yamnaya, Corded Ware, Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age Europeans and earlier farmers/hunter-gatherers
Mainly ~6000–1000 BCE; key Yamnaya/Corded Ware comparison ~3300–2500 BCE
69 newly analysed ancient Europeans (94 libraries); combined analysis includes 25 previously published ancient individuals
390,000-SNP capture; PCA; ADMIXTURE; f3/f4 statistics; ancestry modelling; mtDNA and Y haplogroups

Pontic-Caspian Steppe / Samara-related source
Central Europe and farther west/north
Rapid westward migration and admixture with local Neolithic populations
Approximately 3000–2500 BCE
Large ancestry turnover, admixture and participation of both sexes

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
1. Introduction
Ancient DNA1 has transformed the study of third-millennium BCE mobility2 because it can test whether changes in ancestry accompanied archaeological transitions across Eurasia. Genome-wide ancestry estimates3, identity-by-descent segments4, kinship5, uniparental markers6 and isotope data7 can reveal population relationships and help distinguish long-distance movement from local continuity. These methods are particularly relevant to the Yamnaya horizon8, whose expansion began near the start of the project’s 3300–2600 BCE interval and was followed by major demographic changes both west and east of the Pontic–Caspian Steppe9. The evidence reviewed here supports a broad model of rapid, bidirectional dispersal10 of Yamnaya-related populations after a multi-stage formation process, followed by regionally variable admixture11 and restructuring rather than a single uniform replacement event (Allentoft et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2021).
1 DNA recovered from human remains, such as bones or teeth, dating to the past.2 Here, mobility means the movement of individuals or populations between regions.3 Estimates based on DNA markers across the whole genome that indicate which earlier populations contributed to a person’s ancestry.4 Stretches of DNA shared by people because they inherited them from a relatively recent common ancestor.5 Biological relationships among individuals, such as parent–child or siblings.6 Genetic markers inherited through only one parental line: mitochondrial DNA through the maternal line and the Y chromosome through the paternal line.7 Chemical signatures in teeth or bones that can provide clues about where a person grew up or what they ate.8 A widely distributed Early Bronze Age archaeological phenomenon associated with pastoral communities of the Pontic–Caspian Steppe.9 The grassland region north of the Black Sea and Caspian Sea.10 Movement in two directions—westward into Europe and eastward into Inner Asia.11 The genetic mixing of previously separated populations.12 The boundaries on what the evidence can reasonably demonstrate.13 An estimate of ancestry produced by comparing ancient genomes with selected reference populations.14 The study of how languages change over time and how different languages are historically related.15 Carefully qualified wording that reflects the strength and limits of the available evidence.The inferential limits12 of this evidence are equally important. Ancient genomes directly record biological relationships and modelled ancestry13, not ethnicity, archaeological identity or spoken language. Genetic results can therefore establish that a population moved, mixed or was replaced, while the connection of those processes to Indo-European language dispersal remains an interdisciplinary interpretation. Archaeological context and historical linguistics14 are required to assess whether a demographic expansion also transmitted language. Accordingly, this review distinguishes direct genetic observations from demographic interpretation and then from linguistic inference. It uses calibrated language15 such as “compatible with” or “consistent with” rather than claiming that DNA proves which language an individual spoke (Haak et al., 2015; Tassi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
section: 2. Evidence for Yamnaya population movement across Eurasia
text:
2. Evidence for Yamnaya population movement across Eurasia

2.1 Formation followed by expansion
Evidence immediately preceding 3300 BCE suggests that Yamnaya ancestry did not arise from an isolated or genetically uniform source. Lazaridis et al. (2025) modelled a multi-stage process in which Caucasus–Lower Volga-related ancestry moved west and mixed with Dnipro–Don hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, producing most of the ancestry later found in sampled Yamnaya individuals. Their reconstruction places the formation of a core population before the archaeological expansion and the rapid dispersal after approximately 3300 BCE. Nikitin et al. (2025) provide a complementary North Pontic sequence: Caucasus–Lower Volga-related migrants mixed with Trypillian farmers16 in the formation of Usatove groups, while a parallel mixture with local foragers17 contributed to Serednii Stih populations, from which later Yamnaya groups derived substantial ancestry. Chintalapati et al. (2022), using admixture-date estimates18 across Europe and western Asia, likewise place important Steppe-ancestry formation processes before the archaeological appearance of the Yamnaya and Afanasievo horizons19. These models converge on staged formation followed by expansion, although they do not yet resolve one precise formation centre or every intervening route.
16 Farming communities associated with the Cucuteni–Trypillia archaeological culture of eastern Europe.17 People who obtained food mainly through hunting, fishing and gathering rather than farming.18 Statistical estimates of approximately when two previously distinct populations began mixing.19 The Afanasievo horizon was an Early Bronze Age archaeological phenomenon in the Altai and nearby parts of Inner Asia.Earlier southeastern European evidence provides necessary context but should not be treated as direct evidence for the 3300–2600 BCE migration itself. Mathieson et al. (2018) identified intermittent genetic contact between Steppe and southeastern European populations long before the large third-millennium BCE ancestry shifts. This longer history indicates that the Yamnaya expansion emerged from existing networks of contact rather than initiating east–west interaction. However, the rapidity and scale of the later dispersal distinguish it from these earlier contacts. The chronological distinction is therefore between earlier interaction that contributed to ancestry formation, the Yamnaya expansion beginning around 3300 BCE, and subsequent regional transformations within and after the target interval (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Mathieson et al., 2018; Nikitin et al., 2025).


2.2 Westward movement into Europe
The strongest evidence for Yamnaya-related migration is the large ancestry shift in central and northern Europe near 3000 BCE. Haak et al. (2015) estimated that sampled German Corded Ware20 individuals derived approximately three-quarters of their ancestry from a Yamnaya-related source, a result inconsistent with an explanation based only on the circulation of artefacts or ideas. Allentoft et al. (2015) independently found substantial genetic affinity21 between Yamnaya and Corded Ware groups across their broader Eurasian dataset. More recently, Ringbauer et al. (2024) identified long identity-by-descent segments linking several Corded Ware and Yamnaya groups. Because such long segments indicate relatively recent shared ancestors, these results narrow the demographic connection to only a few hundred years and strengthen the case for rapid movement from the Steppe into central and northern Europe (Allentoft et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2015; Ringbauer et al., 2024).
20 An archaeological phenomenon of third-millennium BCE Europe named after the cord impressions used to decorate pottery.21 Genetic similarity that suggests shared ancestry or historical population connections.This convergence does not mean that every Corded Ware community descended directly from one sampled Yamnaya population. Haak et al. (2015) acknowledged that their Samara Yamnaya sample might not be the precise source, while Ringbauer et al. (2024) identified both recent Yamnaya connections and substantial ancestry related to Globular Amphora populations. Papac et al. (2021) similarly found that Corded Ware groups in Bohemia possessed high but heterogeneous Steppe-related ancestry that could not be explained entirely by the sampled Yamnaya sources. “Yamnaya-related ancestry” is therefore more accurate than assuming descent from a single homogeneous Yamnaya group. The broad westward movement is strongly supported, but the contributing source populations, corridors and number of migration pulses remain less certain (Haak et al., 2015; Papac et al., 2021; Ringbauer et al., 2024).


2.3 Eastward movement into Inner Asia
Ancient DNA also supports an eastward expansion. Allentoft et al. (2015) found Afanasievo individuals from the Altai22 to be genetically close to sampled Yamnaya groups, consistent with rapid movement across a very large distance in the early third millennium BCE. Wang et al. (2021) extended this pattern into western Mongolia and Xinjiang, identifying Yamnaya/Afanasievo-related ancestry after approximately 3000 BCE. Their regional sequence shows that the ancestry later declined in parts of Mongolia while persisting farther west, demonstrating that eastward dispersal was followed by local admixture and population turnover23 rather than permanent demographic uniformity. Chintalapati et al. (2022) provide a broader chronological framework compatible with the formation and later spread of this ancestry.
22 A mountain region in Inner Asia where Russia, Mongolia, China and Kazakhstan meet.23 A substantial change in a region’s population through migration, replacement or mixing.The eastern evidence is less geographically continuous than the evidence from central Europe. Genetic similarity between Yamnaya and Afanasievo populations supports a broad eastward dispersal, but sparsely sampled intermediate areas limit reconstruction of the exact route. Archaeological labels also cannot substitute for ancestry: Wang et al. (2021) report that an Afanasievo-associated context did not invariably correspond to Yamnaya-related genetic ancestry. The most defensible conclusion is therefore that closely related populations moved east toward the Altai, western Mongolia and Xinjiang after about 3000 BCE, while the detailed corridors and correspondence between archaeological and genetic classifications remain provisional (Allentoft et al., 2015; Chintalapati et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
3. Routes, chronology and demographic consequences

3.1 A sequence rather than a single event
Across the evidence, Yamnaya-associated mobility is best understood as a sequence. Earlier mixtures in the Caucasus–Lower Volga, Dnipro–Don, North Pontic and southeastern European interaction zones supplied the ancestry and social connections from which expansion emerged. Direct target-period evidence then documents westward and eastward movement beginning around 3300–3000 BCE. Finally, regional studies record assimilation, further turnover and long-distance continuities during the later target period and after 2600 BCE (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Mathieson et al., 2018; Nikitin et al., 2025). This sequence prevents later transformations—particularly Bell Beaker-period changes—from being projected backwards as direct evidence about Yamnaya communities.
The Corded Ware relationship illustrates both the strength and uncertainty of route reconstruction. Genome-wide ancestry and identity-by-descent evidence support rapid, recent genealogical connections with Yamnaya-related populations, but the sampled Yamnaya groups need not represent the only source. Corded Ware populations also incorporated ancestry related to earlier European groups and differed between regions. The data therefore favour substantial population movement followed by local admixture over either a purely cultural diffusion model or a uniform replacement by one genetically homogeneous migrant population (Haak et al., 2015; Papac et al., 2021; Ringbauer et al., 2024).


3.2 Replacement, admixture and regional restructuring
Regional time series24 show that the demographic consequences of Steppe migration varied markedly. In Bohemia, Corded Ware populations appeared by approximately 2900 BCE with high but variable Steppe-related ancestry, after which the incorporation of women with diverse ancestry and sharp changes in Y-chromosome lineages25 indicate repeated social and genetic restructuring. Some of the most pronounced changes occurred around 2600 BCE or later, so they represent the end of the target interval and its consequences rather than the initial Yamnaya expansion (Papac et al., 2021). In southeastern Poland, genomic, kinship and strontium-isotope data26 instead reveal a smaller-scale pattern in which Steppe-associated paternal ancestry coexisted with maternal lineages27 related to earlier Neolithic populations, including kin relationships that crossed local and non-local mobility categories (Linderholm et al., 2020). Together, these studies replace a single model of “mass migration” with evidence for multiple combinations of long-distance movement, local incorporation and community reorganisation.
24 Genetic samples from the same region but from different periods, allowing researchers to track change over time.25 Lines of paternal descent traced through variants of the Y chromosome.26 Measurements of strontium in teeth that can help determine whether a person grew up locally or moved from another geological region.27 Lines of descent traced through mothers, commonly studied using mitochondrial DNA.28 A migration in which males and females participated in different proportions.29 Relating to the non-sex chromosomes, which are inherited from both parents.30 Relating to the X chromosome, whose inheritance pattern differs between males and females.31 The proportion and depth of an ancient genome successfully recovered through DNA sequencing.The migration was often sex-biased28, but its magnitude cannot be assumed to have been constant across Eurasia. Scorrano et al. (2021) found stronger male bias in Steppe-related ancestry among several Corded Ware groups than among Bell Beaker groups, using autosomal29, X-chromosomal30 and uniparental comparisons. Linderholm et al. (2020) and Papac et al. (2021) likewise identify patterns consistent with male-linked Steppe ancestry and the incorporation of local or genetically diverse women. Nevertheless, these conclusions are best resolved in parts of central Europe and southeastern Poland, and some estimates are limited by small sample sizes, uneven genome coverage31 and low X-chromosome marker counts. Sex-biased mobility is thus a recurring regional mechanism, not a securely quantified Eurasia-wide constant (Linderholm et al., 2020; Papac et al., 2021; Scorrano et al., 2021).
Later Bell Beaker evidence32 further demonstrates why archaeological culture and population movement must be separated. Olalde et al. (2018) found limited genetic affinity between Iberian and central European Beaker-associated groups, suggesting that some shared material practices spread without equivalent population movement. In Britain, by contrast, Beaker-associated migration introduced high Steppe-related ancestry and replaced approximately 90% of the existing gene pool33 within a few centuries. This British transformation mainly postdates 2600 BCE and is therefore a consequence of earlier Steppe-related dispersal rather than direct evidence for the initial Yamnaya migration. Tassi et al. (2017) provide a complementary earlier case: Globular Amphora34 individuals in northwestern Poland were genetically closer to earlier Neolithic populations and lacked the expected Yamnaya-derived profile despite eastern archaeological affinities. Taken together, these results show that material culture can spread through cultural transmission in one context and accompany major demographic change in another (Olalde et al., 2018; Tassi et al., 2017).
32 Evidence associated with the Bell Beaker phenomenon, named after its distinctive bell-shaped pottery.33 The total collection of genetic variation present in a population.34 A Late Neolithic archaeological culture of central and eastern Europe named after its rounded pottery vessels.

text:
4. Migration and Indo-European language dispersal

4.1 A compatible demographic mechanism
The scale and speed of Yamnaya-related movement provide a credible demographic mechanism through which languages could have dispersed. Haak et al. (2015) interpreted the major Steppe-derived ancestry influx into central Europe as support for a Steppe-origin model for at least some Indo-European languages, while explicitly acknowledging that genetic data are silent about the language spoken by sampled individuals. Allentoft et al. (2015) similarly described the bidirectional genomic transformations of Bronze Age Eurasia as consistent with a proposed early Bronze Age dispersal of Indo-European languages. These conclusions are meaningful because large movements of people create opportunities for language transmission, but they do not demonstrate that population replacement and language replacement occurred at the same rate or through the same social process.
The reviewed studies vary in how directly they discuss language. Some make explicit linguistic interpretations of their demographic results, whereas others supply indirect evidence about migration chronology, scale, sex bias or social incorporation. The latter studies should not be presented as independent confirmation of a linguistic hypothesis. For example, identity-by-descent links between Yamnaya and Corded Ware groups strengthen the evidence for recent population movement, but do not identify the language of either group (Ringbauer et al., 2024). Likewise, sex-biased ancestry and kinship structures may help reconstruct how migrants were incorporated, but they cannot show which languages were used within households or transmitted to later generations (Linderholm et al., 2020; Papac et al., 2021; Scorrano et al., 2021).


4.2 Eastward dispersal and the proto-Tocharian interpretation
The eastward Yamnaya–Afanasievo connection has particular relevance to proposals concerning proto-Tocharian35. Wang et al. (2021) argue that the movement of a population closely related to Yamnaya into the Altai and farther into Inner Asia adds weight to a migration-mediated account of proto-Tocharian dispersal. Allentoft et al. (2015) and Chintalapati et al. (2022) provide supporting demographic and chronological context for this eastward movement. However, “proto-Tocharian” is a linguistic interpretation applied to the demographic pattern, not a genetic measurement. Sparse sampling along intermediate routes and the imperfect correspondence between Afanasievo archaeological contexts and Yamnaya-related ancestry make a one-to-one mapping between population movement and language branch unjustified (Allentoft et al., 2015; Chintalapati et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).
35 The reconstructed ancestor of the extinct Tocharian languages once spoken in parts of the Tarim Basin.36 A proposed ancestral stage before the Anatolian languages separated from the other Indo-European branches.Broader proposals about Indo-European roots require the same caution. Lazaridis et al. (2025) connect their reconstruction of Caucasus–Lower Volga and North Pontic ancestry formation to a model of proto-Indo-Anatolian unity36 before Yamnaya expansion and later language branching. This is the collection’s most explicit integration of genetic, archaeological and linguistic reasoning, but the linguistic conclusion remains dependent on the demographic model and independent linguistic assumptions. The unresolved location of some source populations and routes, including proposed connections towards Anatolia, prevents genetic models alone from determining a language homeland. Tassi et al. (2017) reinforce this limitation from the opposite direction: an archaeological group can display eastern cultural affinities without the expected Steppe ancestry, and language change need not follow demographic movement exactly. Genetic evidence can therefore test whether a proposed language-spread model has a plausible population mechanism, but it cannot adjudicate language identity by itself (Lazaridis et al., 2025; Tassi et al., 2017).

section: 5. Limits of linking genes, archaeological culture and language
text:
5. Limits of linking genes, archaeological culture and language
The broad directions of Yamnaya-related movement are more secure than their fine-grained routes. Ancient-DNA models depend on the populations available as ancestry proxies37, and unsampled groups may have contributed to both Yamnaya and Corded Ware populations. Admixture-date methods can also compress several closely spaced movements into an approximate date, while identity-by-descent detection depends on genome coverage and performs most reliably for longer segments. These constraints do not overturn the evidence for rapid dispersal, but they limit claims about a single point of origin, a unique migration corridor or an exact number of pulses38 (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Nikitin et al., 2025; Ringbauer et al., 2024).
37 Sampled populations used as stand-ins when estimating the ancestry of another population.38 Separate episodes or waves of migration.39 A sequence of samples collected across a geographic route or a series of locations.The evidence is geographically and chronologically uneven. Central and northern Europe contain comparatively dense regional and community-level datasets, whereas the lower Volga, North Pontic–Caucasus zones, northern Eurasia and intermediate Inner Asian corridors remain less continuously sampled. Research using modern northern Eurasian genomes and published ancient comparators provides context for older Siberian–European interactions, but cannot substitute for a direct transect39 of Yamnaya-period individuals (Wong et al., 2017). Similarly, studies spanning millennia must isolate the 3300–2600 BCE evidence from earlier ancestry formation and later Bronze Age consequences. Without this separation, later replacement or modern-population affinity can be mistaken for direct evidence about Yamnaya migration (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Mathieson et al., 2018; Olalde et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2017).
Most importantly, ancestry, archaeological culture, ethnicity and language are distinct analytical categories. An individual may be buried in a Corded Ware or Afanasievo context without possessing a uniform ancestry profile, and a population may adopt material practices without large-scale genetic change. Conversely, a substantial ancestry shift demonstrates migration but does not reveal whether incoming languages replaced, coexisted with or were adopted by local populations. None of the genetic studies reviewed contains a direct linguistic dataset capable of testing speech, branching, borrowing or multilingualism. Ancient DNA can therefore support or constrain demographic scenarios associated with Indo-European dispersal, but the linguistic argument ultimately requires independent historical-linguistic and archaeological evidence (Tassi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
6. Synthesis and research gaps
Ancient DNA provides strong evidence that Yamnaya-related mobility was a major Eurasian demographic process during 3300–2600 BCE. The most coherent reconstruction is a multi-stage formation process involving interaction among Caucasus–Lower Volga-related, Dnipro–Don/North Pontic and neighbouring populations, followed by rapid expansion from approximately 3300 BCE. Westward movement into central and northern Europe is supported by large ancestry shifts and recent genealogical links, while the genetic relationship between Yamnaya and Afanasievo populations supports a parallel eastward movement towards the Altai and Inner Asia. In both directions, migration was followed by regionally different mixtures of incorporation, sex bias, continuity and replacement rather than a single uniform process (Allentoft et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Nikitin et al., 2025; Papac et al., 2021; Ringbauer et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2021).
Several questions remain unresolved. Direct sampling is still insufficient to define every lower-Volga, North Pontic, Caucasus or possible Anatolian route, and intermediate populations between the Pontic–Caspian Steppe and Inner Asia remain sparse. Source substructure40 and chronological resolution41 make it difficult to distinguish one large migration from several closely spaced movements. Community-level studies of kinship, mobility and sex bias are concentrated in a limited number of European settings, restricting comparison across Eurasia. More matched archaeological–genetic transects are needed to determine when similar material cultures reflect population movement, local adoption or mixed processes (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Linderholm et al., 2020; Nikitin et al., 2025; Papac et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
40 Genetic differences among smaller groups within what might otherwise be treated as one source population.41 How precisely the available evidence can distinguish events occurring at different times.The largest interpretive gap concerns language. The demographic expansion is compatible with some Steppe-based models of Indo-European dispersal and supplies a plausible mechanism for moving languages across large distances. It does not, however, establish the speech of Yamnaya, Corded Ware or Afanasievo individuals, nor does it independently resolve language homelands, branches or transmission mechanisms. The defensible conclusion is therefore two-part: ancient DNA strongly supports rapid bidirectional dispersal of Yamnaya-related populations and subsequent regional restructuring, while any connection between those movements and particular Indo-European languages remains an interdisciplinary inference rather than a direct genetic finding (Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Tassi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
section: The whole story in one paragraph
text:
The whole story in one paragraph
Long before the Yamnaya expansion, people living around the Steppe, the lower Volga, the Caucasus, the North Pontic region and southeastern Europe were already meeting and mixing. Over time, these contacts helped form the ancestry later found in Yamnaya groups. At about 3300 BCE, Yamnaya-related people began moving very quickly in two broad directions: west into Europe and east towards the Altai and Inner Asia. Their movement changed the genetic history of many regions, but it did not have the same result everywhere. In some places there was large population change. In others, newcomers mixed with local people. Sometimes men appear to have moved more than women. Sometimes archaeological objects and customs spread without a large movement of people. These population movements could have helped spread Indo-European languages, but DNA cannot tell us what language any ancient person spoke. The safest conclusion is therefore: ancient DNA strongly supports rapid Yamnaya-related migration, but the connection to particular Indo-European languages remains a careful interpretation, not a direct genetic fact.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
section: 1. Before the journey: the Yamnaya did not appear from nowhere
text:
1. Before the journey: the Yamnaya did not appear from nowhere
Imagine the story beginning before there was a fully formed Yamnaya population.
The lands around the Pontic–Caspian Steppe were not empty or isolated. People had been moving, meeting and mixing there for a long time. Mathieson et al. (2018) found evidence of contact between Steppe populations and southeastern Europe well before the main Yamnaya expansion. Wong et al. (2017) also found signs of older connections between western Siberia, the Urals and northeastern Europe. These studies remind us that east–west contact did not suddenly begin in 3300 BCE.
The most detailed recent studies describe Yamnaya formation as a process with several stages. Lazaridis et al. (2025) argue that ancestry related to the Caucasus and lower Volga moved west and mixed with people connected to the Dnipro and Don areas. Nikitin et al. (2025) describe several movements and mixtures in the North Pontic region. They connect Caucasus–Lower Volga-related people, Trypillian farmers, local foragers, Usatove groups, Serednii Stih groups and later Yamnaya populations.
The simple meaning is this: Yamnaya ancestry was built through earlier movement and mixture. It was not created by one isolated, unchanging tribe.
Chintalapati et al. (2022) help place these events in time. Their study suggests that important mixtures happened before the archaeological Yamnaya horizon became visible. The genetic population was therefore developing before the famous expansion began.
There is still uncertainty. The studies broadly agree on a multi-stage formation process, but they do not identify one perfectly certain birthplace or every exact route. Some possible source populations have not yet been sampled. The lower Volga, Don–Dnipro region, North Caucasus and routes towards Anatolia still need more evidence.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
section: 2. The launch: rapid movement after about 3300 BCE
text:
2. The launch: rapid movement after about 3300 BCE
After this long formation process, something changed. From about 3300 BCE, Yamnaya-related populations began to spread rapidly across a very large area.
This was not movement in only one direction. The broad pattern was bidirectional:

westwards into central and northern Europe; and
eastwards towards the Altai, western Mongolia and Xinjiang.

Allentoft et al. (2015) is important because it shows both sides of this pattern. The study found strong genetic connections between Yamnaya and Corded Ware populations in the west, and between Yamnaya and Afanasievo populations in the east. This makes the Yamnaya story a Eurasian story, not only a European one.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
section: 3. The westward road: movement into Europe
text:
3. The westward road: movement into Europe
The strongest part of the evidence concerns movement west into Europe.
Haak et al. (2015) found that sampled German Corded Ware people had a very large amount of ancestry related to sampled Yamnaya people. Their estimate was roughly three-quarters. A change this large is very difficult to explain through the movement of objects or ideas alone. It points to a substantial movement of people from the Steppe into central Europe around 3000 BCE.
Allentoft et al. (2015) reached a similar broad conclusion using a different Eurasian dataset. The agreement between these early major studies made rapid Steppe-related migration into Europe one of the clearest findings in ancient-DNA research.
Ringbauer et al. (2024) later added another kind of evidence. The researchers examined long pieces of DNA shared by ancient individuals. These pieces are called identity-by-descent, or IBD, segments. In simple language, a long shared segment means that two people or populations had fairly recent common ancestors. Corded Ware and Yamnaya groups shared segments showing connections within only a few hundred years. This makes the movement look rapid and recent, rather than the result of a very distant shared ancestor.
However, we should not imagine that every Corded Ware person came directly from one sampled Yamnaya group. Papac et al. (2021) found that Corded Ware populations in Bohemia had high but varied Steppe-related ancestry. They were not genetically or socially identical. Ringbauer et al. (2024) also found ancestry connected to earlier European groups such as Globular Amphora populations.
This is why the phrase “Yamnaya-related ancestry” is safer than saying that every Corded Ware community was simply Yamnaya. The broad family connection and westward movement are strong. The exact source groups and routes are less certain.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
text:
4. What happened after migrants arrived
The newcomers did not enter an empty Europe. They met local people. Different regions then developed in different ways.
Papac et al. (2021) show this clearly in Bohemia. Corded Ware populations arrived with high Steppe-related ancestry, but they also incorporated women from different local backgrounds. Later changes in male family lines suggest further social and population restructuring. This was not one simple replacement followed by stability.
Linderholm et al. (2020) provide a smaller, community-level view from southeastern Poland. Their genomic, family-relationship and isotope evidence suggests a mixture of Steppe-associated paternal ancestry and maternal lines connected to earlier Neolithic populations. Local and non-local people could even appear within the same family network.
Scorrano et al. (2021) examined whether Steppe migration was sex-biased. Several Corded Ware datasets appear to show a stronger movement of men than women. However, the strength of this pattern varies between places, and some of the genetic estimates are uncertain. The safe conclusion is not “only men migrated.” It is: male-biased migration appears to have been an important mechanism in some European regions, alongside the incorporation of local women.
These regional studies change the shape of the story. There was a large westward migration, but there was no single result everywhere. The real pattern included migration, mixture, marriage, local incorporation, family movement and repeated population change.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
section: 5. Objects, cultures and people are not the same thing
text:
5. Objects, cultures and people are not the same thing
Archaeologists give names such as Yamnaya, Corded Ware, Globular Amphora and Bell Beaker to patterns of burials, pottery and other material remains. These names are useful, but they do not automatically describe one biological population.
Tassi et al. (2017) provide an important negative example. People from a Globular Amphora burial in Poland had cultural links looking towards the east, but they did not have the expected Yamnaya-related genetic profile. This suggests that ideas and objects could spread without a matching mass movement of people.
Olalde et al. (2018) show both possibilities within the Bell Beaker world. Iberian and central European Beaker groups shared material culture but had limited genetic similarity. In that case, practices probably travelled more strongly than people. Britain was different. Beaker-associated migration brought a large amount of Steppe-related ancestry and replaced about 90% of the earlier gene pool within a few centuries. Much of this British change occurred after 2600 BCE, so it is best understood as a later consequence of Steppe-related dispersal rather than direct evidence about the first Yamnaya expansion.
Furholt (2018) gives the broader warning behind these examples. We should not turn archaeological cultures into simple, uniform “peoples.” A shared pot, burial custom or cultural label does not prove that everyone belonged to one ancestry group, moved together or spoke the same language.
The lesson is simple: sometimes culture moved with people, and sometimes culture moved between people. We have to test each place separately.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
section: 6. The eastward road: movement into Inner Asia
text:
6. The eastward road: movement into Inner Asia
The second great road led east.
Allentoft et al. (2015) found that Afanasievo individuals from the Altai were genetically very close to sampled Yamnaya groups. The great distance between the Steppe and the Altai suggests rapid eastward movement in the early third millennium BCE.
Wang et al. (2021) followed this story farther into Asia. Yamnaya/Afanasievo-related ancestry appeared in western Mongolia after about 3000 BCE and later reached or persisted in areas farther west, including Xinjiang. The ancestry did not remain equally strong everywhere. In parts of Mongolia it later declined as populations mixed and changed.
The broad eastward movement is well supported, but the road between the Steppe and Inner Asia is not filled with evenly spaced samples. We are missing many intermediate populations. Also, an archaeological site labelled Afanasievo does not always contain people with the ancestry researchers might expect.
The safe picture is therefore: a population closely related to Yamnaya moved rapidly east towards the Altai and Inner Asia, but the exact route and every local stage remain uncertain.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
section: 7. The Caucasus and northern Eurasia: important background roads
text:
7. The Caucasus and northern Eurasia: important background roads
The Caucasus was not simply a wall separating north and south. It could also act as a corridor through which people and ancestry moved.
Dzhaubermezov et al. (2026) bring together a large body of Caucasus research. Their review describes long-term regional continuity together with periods of Steppe-related gene flow and mixture. Because it combines previously published datasets and covers a very long period, it is best used as supporting context rather than as one direct Yamnaya migration route. The workbook also flagged its publication-date metadata for checking before final submission.
Wong et al. (2017) provide similar broad context for northern Eurasia. Their study is based mainly on modern northern populations together with published ancient comparisons. It suggests deep connections between Siberia, the Urals and northeastern Europe. It is useful for showing that the wider region had a long history of movement, but it is not a direct line of Yamnaya-period graves leading from one place to another.
Together, these studies stop the story from becoming too simple. Yamnaya expansion was important, but it occurred inside a much older network of Eurasian connections.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
section: 8. Were horses the engine of the first expansion?
text:
8. Were horses the engine of the first expansion?
Horses are often placed at the centre of popular Yamnaya stories. Librado et al. (2021), however, found that the horse lineage that later spread widely did not drive the first movement of human Steppe ancestry into Europe. The great expansion of those domestic horses happened later.
This does not mean horses were unimportant in all later Steppe societies. It means we should not automatically explain the first Yamnaya migration by saying, “They had the later domestic horse system, so they could spread.” The timing does not fit that simple story.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
Yamnaya Lit Review
text:
10. The final picture
The story begins with long-term contact. Different populations around the Caucasus, lower Volga, North Pontic region and Steppe mixed over many generations. From this process, Yamnaya-related ancestry formed.
At about 3300 BCE, Yamnaya-related populations began a rapid expansion. One stream moved west into Europe. Another moved east towards the Altai and Inner Asia.
The western movement is the strongest part of the evidence. Large ancestry changes and close genetic family connections link Yamnaya-related and Corded Ware populations. Yet Corded Ware communities were not all the same, and sampled Yamnaya groups may not represent the one exact source.
After arrival, the results differed by region. Some places experienced major population turnover. Others show admixture and local continuity. In several European settings, migration was male-biased and included the incorporation of local women. Material culture sometimes moved with populations and sometimes spread without large genetic change.
The eastern movement is also supported, especially through the close Yamnaya–Afanasievo relationship. However, the intermediate route is more sparsely sampled than the European route.
These migrations could have helped Indo-European languages spread. They provide the people-moving mechanism that a language-spread model needs. But they do not reveal speech. Language conclusions must therefore be built by combining genetics with archaeology and historical linguistics.

title: Yamnaya Lit Review
text:
The memory version
If you need to remember the literature review quickly, hold these six lines in your mind:

Formation: Yamnaya ancestry formed through earlier movement and mixture.
Launch: Rapid expansion began around 3300 BCE.
Two roads: People moved west into Europe and east into Inner Asia.
Different endings: Each region had a different mixture of replacement, continuity and local incorporation.
Culture is not DNA: Similar objects do not always mean the same population moved.
DNA is not language: Migration could spread language, but genetics cannot identify speech.

Tier

S001
Haak et al. (2015)
Core
Westward migration; language
Corded Ware individuals derived about 75% of their ancestry from Yamnaya-related groups about 2,600 km east, supporting a large third-millennium migration into central Europe.
The language link is an inference from genetic, archaeological and chronological agreement.


S002
Allentoft et al. (2015)
Core
Westward and eastward expansion; language
Genomes from 101 ancient Eurasians link Yamnaya-related movement westward and Afanasievo movement eastward to large Bronze Age population shifts.
Broad sampling masks local variation; language is not observed genetically.


S004
Sjögren et al. (2016)
Contextual
Mobility mechanism
First-generation mobility was high in two Corded Ware cemeteries in southern Germany, especially among women, consistent with sustained female exogamy after the steppe-related expansion.
Isotopes identify non-local people but rarely locate their place of origin; no new ancient DNA was generated.


S007
Saag et al. (2017)
Core
Northeastern route; sex bias
The first farmers sampled in Estonia carried predominantly steppe ancestry, indicating migration into the eastern Baltic and sex-specific admixture with farmer-related groups.
The result is based on ten individuals from one regional transect.


S008
Tassi et al. (2017)
Contextual
Population interaction; language
Globular Amphora individuals lacked Yamnaya-related ancestry, whereas later Corded Ware and Bell Beaker groups retained a direct maternal connection to Yamnaya populations.
The sampled Globular Amphora sites may not represent the entire cultural complex; linguistic implications remain indirect.


S010
Nikitin et al. (2017)
Core
North Pontic continuity
Western North Pontic mitochondrial lineages show continuity from Eneolithic groups into Yamnaya and later Early Bronze Age groups, with two Yamnaya individuals carrying an eastern Eurasian lineage.
Twelve mitochondrial sequences provide limited resolution and cannot reconstruct total population movement.


S011
Fernandes et al. (2018)
Contextual
Central European admixture
Steppe ancestry appeared in Corded Ware individuals in north-central Poland but with a smaller contribution and more local hunter-gatherer ancestry than in other regions.
Seventeen individuals from one region limit wider generalization.


S013
Hollard et al. (2018)
Core
Eastward Afanasievo route
Uniparental markers support a genetic link between Afanasievo and Yamnaya populations, but the data do not support an Afanasievo paternal migration into the Tarim Basin.
Small samples and uniparental markers cannot resolve all migration routes.


S014
Olalde et al. (2018)
Contextual
Later westward expansion
The initial Beaker spread between Iberia and central Europe was mainly cultural, but later Beaker-associated migration carried steppe ancestry to Britain and replaced about 90% of its gene pool.
Most of the demographic change occurred after 2600 BCE and concerns Yamnaya-derived populations.


S015
Mathieson et al. (2018)
Core
Southeastern European corridor
Southeastern Europe was a long-term contact zone; steppe-related gene flow preceded the major third-millennium migration, and western Yamnaya individuals show local southeastern European admixture.
The study covers a long period, and proposed language scenarios are interpretive.


S016
Malmström et al. (2019)
Core
Scandinavian route
Battle Axe individuals carried substantial Pontic-Caspian steppe ancestry that requires migration into Scandinavia, followed by mixture with resident farmers.
Only a small number of Battle Axe individuals was available.


S017
Schroeder et al. (2019)
Contextual
Coexistence and possible conflict
A contemporaneous Globular Amphora family lacked steppe ancestry, showing that local populations remained genetically distinct during Corded Ware expansion.
A link between the massacre and incoming Corded Ware groups is possible but unproven.


S018
Linderholm et al. (2020)
Contextual
Regional admixture; sex bias
Corded Ware individuals in southeastern Poland combined paternal steppe signals with maternal Neolithic lineages, and genomic-isotopic evidence linked local and non-local relatives.
The authors caution that sample size and genomic coverage limit inference.


S019
Racimo et al. (2020)
Core
Migration direction and speed
Spatial modelling identifies a westward expansion from the Caspian steppe at about 4.2 km per year using a 50% ancestry threshold, at least twice the estimated Neolithic rate.
Speed estimates depend on ancestry thresholds, the assumed origin and uneven ancient-genome coverage.


S021
Ochir-Goryaeva et al. (2021)
Contextual
Yamnaya-Catacomb continuity
Two Catacomb males carried paternal and maternal lineages also found among Yamnaya individuals, consistent with continuity in the eastern European steppe after the focal period.
Two uniparental profiles can suggest, but cannot establish, close population continuity.


S022
Papac et al. (2021)
Contextual
Central European diversity
Corded Ware groups appeared in Bohemia by about 2900 BCE, were initially diverse, did not obtain all steppe ancestry from sampled Yamnaya groups, and incorporated women from varied backgrounds.
A dense regional transect does not by itself identify the unsampled steppe source.


S024
Wang et al. (2021)
Core
Eastward route; proto-Tocharian
Yamnaya-derived Afanasievo ancestry reached western Mongolia after about 3000 BCE, later declined there, and persisted farther west in China in a pattern compatible with proto-Tocharian dispersal.
The proto-Tocharian association is a multidisciplinary inference, not a genetic observation.


S025
Egfjord et al. (2021)
Contextual
Northern European expansion
Single Grave Culture individuals in Denmark carried substantial Yamnaya-derived ancestry, opposing demographic continuity with the preceding Funnel Beaker population.
Only three partial genomes were recovered, and broader representativeness is uncertain.


S027
Rio et al. (2021)
Core
Migration mechanism
Simulations favour rare long-distance movement, prolonged farmer-pastoralist cohabitation and limited admixture during expansion from the Pontic steppe into central Europe.
Results depend on model structure and ancestry estimates drawn from published genomes.


S028
Scorrano et al. (2021)
Core
Sex-biased migration
Reanalysis indicates a male-biased steppe contribution in central European Corded Ware groups and a weaker bias in Bell Beaker groups, with little detectable mitochondrial replacement.
The analysis inherits geographic and preservation biases from published datasets.


S031
Kroonen et al. (2022)
Core
Linguistic homeland
Reconstructed cereal vocabulary places core Indo-European in a mixed agro-pastoral setting, making western Yamnaya near or west of the Dnieper a better linguistic proxy than early eastern Yamnaya.
This is linguistic evidence; etymological reconstruction and archaeological matching remain contestable.


S032
Broccard et al. (2022)
Contextual
Demographic turnover
Mitochondrial simulations find that substantial post-Neolithic immigration, explicitly modelled from the Pontic steppe, best explains central European genetic discontinuity.
Mitochondrial data cannot uniquely identify the source, timing or sex composition of the migration.


S034
Chintalapati et al. (2022)
Core
Admixture chronology; language
Admixture dating places Yamnaya-Afanasievo genetic formation around 4400-4000 BCE and indicates rapid, near-synchronous Corded Ware mixture across Europe around 3000-2900 BCE.
Dates assume simplified admixture histories and remain sensitive to sparse sampling and source choice.


S035
Gerber et al. (2023)
Contextual
Carpathian Basin turnover
Western Hungarian genomes show high steppe ancestry in Somogyvár-Vinkovci groups, followed by replacement by a population with unusually high hunter-gatherer ancestry.
The study is regional and much of its sample falls after the focal Yamnaya period.


S039
Ghalichi et al. (2024)
Core
Caucasus-steppe interaction
Genomes from the Caucasus show that steppe ancestry formed during Eneolithic interaction across the mountain-steppe boundary, followed by Early Bronze Age pastoralist expansion with relative genetic stability.
The wide temporal scope emphasizes formation and regional interaction more than long-distance dispersal.


S040
Nikitin et al. (2025)
Core
North Pontic formation and expansion
Three migration waves entered the North Pontic region; Caucasus-Lower Volga migrants helped form Serednii Stih, whose descendants formed Yamnaya around 4000 BCE and expanded after 3300 BCE.
Ancestry models depend on the available reference populations and geographic sampling.


S042
Roca-Rada et al. (2025)
Contextual
Western endpoint; sex bias
Early Bronze Age Catalans combined local continuity with steppe-related ancestry along a southward Iberian gradient; an eastern European maternal lineage argues against an exclusively male migration.
The evidence comes from a small number of people at one site.


S044
Bourgeois et al. (2025)
Contextual
Cultural versus genetic spread
Radiocarbon modelling shows that Corded Ware and Bell Beaker burial practices spread rapidly and were not synchronized with the east-west spread of steppe ancestry; Corded Ware practices consolidated near 2600 BCE.
The study adds archaeological chronology but relies on published genetic arrival models.


S045
Roca-Rada et al. (2025)
Contextual
Western Eurasian endpoint
Portuguese Bronze Age genomes retain substantial local ancestry despite North Pontic steppe input, showing that the westward expansion produced regional admixture rather than uniform replacement.
The 5,000-year transect gives limited attention to the focal Bronze Age interval.


S046
Lazaridis et al. (2025)
Core
Formation routes; Indo-Anatolian
Caucasus-Lower Volga ancestry moved west and mixed with Dnipro-Don foragers to form Serednii Stih, ancestral to Yamnaya; related movement into Anatolia supports a proposed proto-Indo-Anatolian link.
The language assignment is inferential and the demographic model depends on sampled proxies.


S048
Olalde et al. (2026)
Contextual
Cultural adoption and later expansion
Lower Rhine communities adopted Corded Ware practices with little steppe gene flow; later fusion with migrants of both sexes formed Beaker groups that expanded into northwestern Europe and Britain.
The study concerns a regional exception and much of the expansion post-dates 2600 BCE.


S051
Zhao et al. (2026)
Core
Xinjiang route
Afanasievo-related ancestry entered northwestern Xinjiang in the Early Bronze Age alongside Central Asian ancestry, identifying the Inner Asian Mountain Corridor as an eastward migration route.
Ten individuals from one site limit temporal and regional resolution; language was not tested.

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
1. Defining the problem

1.1 Scope and boundaries

Focus on population movement across Eurasia during 3300–2600 BCE and its possible relationship to language dispersal.
Distinguish evidence that falls directly within the target period from earlier evidence concerning population formation and later evidence concerning demographic consequences.
Discuss origins, archaeological culture and genetic formation only where they contribute to the migration and language argument.



1.2 Types of evidence and their limits

Ancient genomes, ancestry models, identity-by-descent analysis, kinship studies, uniparental markers and relevant isotope evidence provide the main evidence for population movement.5
Migration, admixture and replacement are demographic interpretations drawn from these data.
Archaeological evidence can help reconstruct the context and possible routes of movement, but similarities in material culture do not by themselves demonstrate migration.
Linguistic conclusions require a further interpretive step because language cannot be observed directly in ancient DNA.
